Where it began

Aravinda de Silva was born in Colombo on 17 October 1965 and went to school at D. S. Senanayake College and Isipathana College in the city. He was playing for Sri Lanka at 18: his one-day debut came against New Zealand at Moratuwa in March 1984, and his first Test followed that August, at Lord's against England.

The player

In his early years he was all dash and daring, and he earned the nickname Mad Max for his habit of going after the bowling whatever the situation. He saw no reason to change, and the runs came anyway. He played 93 Tests between 1984 and 2002 and made 6,361 runs at 42.98, with 20 hundreds and 22 fifties. His best was 267 against New Zealand at the Basin Reserve in 1991.

A summer with Kent in 1995, when he made six hundreds and the highest score of the English season, 255, turned out to be the moment it all came together. The best was saved for 1996. In the World Cup final against Australia he took three wickets, including the captain, held two catches and then made 107 not out to win the trophy for Sri Lanka by seven wickets.

What made him special

He liked to take on the best attacks, and the best attacks rarely enjoyed it. Against Pakistan, whose bowlers in his time included Imran Khan, Wasim Akram and Waqar Younis, he made eight hundreds, more than anyone else. In 1997 in Colombo he became the first batsman to make two unbeaten hundreds in the same Test, and twice in his career he made a century in each innings.

His bowling was a useful extra rather than a weapon. He took 29 Test wickets at 44.45, and at Kent he was tidy with the ball without often taking wickets, though he did pick one up with the last ball he ever bowled in a Test.

Away from the middle

He was one of Wisden's five Cricketers of the Year in 1996, and Wisden's list of the 100 finest batting performances includes six of his innings. In 2023 he entered the ICC Cricket Hall of Fame, the fourth Sri Lankan to do so. After retiring in 2003 he served Sri Lankan cricket in several roles, twice as chairman of the national selectors, and in 2007 he turned out for a club side in Dorset as a favour to a friend.

And finally

He finished his Test career against Bangladesh in Colombo in 2002 with a double hundred in his last innings and a wicket with his last ball. Most cricketers would settle for one of those as a farewell.
